svg.title: Where were the Mesopotamian gods born?
svg.desc: Cult seats and separately identified birth traditions. Full source data accompanies this image.
svg.text: Ancient birth traditions—and the cities the gods called home.
Most pins mark cult seats, not births. Local traditions changed across texts and centuries.

g.text: Sippar · solar cult. A hymn places Utu’s birth in
E-nun-ana; identifying that shrine with Sippar is an
Babylon · Esagil’s divine couple. Marduk is born in the
cosmic Apsu in Enuma Elish—not at this city pin. [8]
Borsippa · Ezida and its divine pair. Nabu’s other consort
Dilbat · a male agricultural god and his consort; this
Urash is distinct from the earth goddess. [8]
Marad · the city’s divine lord. His temple is the “House,
Isin · healing goddess and her son. Later
healing-goddess identifications do not erase local
Uruk · several divine households. Nanaya is separately
Larsa · Ebabbar, a major solar sanctuary. A second cult
seat is not a second god. [1]
Bad-tibira · the shepherd god’s E-mush, celebrated as
Nanna’s principal cult city. Ninazu’s hymn says he is
born here, then takes his seat at Enegi. [1,2,5]
Enki’s cult seat. Nanshe’s hymn places her birth here;
her cult home lies at Nigin. [1,4,8]
Eshnunna · the Temple Hymns praise Ninazu here;
Tishpak later holds the leading local position. [1,2]
Der · a divine judge, whose shrine is the “Great Pole
Kutha · lord of Meslam and the underworld.
Meslamtaea is identified with him in this hymn. [1]
Kish · the warrior god’s E-dub. The hymn praises his
power; it does not narrate his birth. [1]
Enlil’s divine court. The canal scene locates Nanna’s
Adab · the mother goddess’s E-mah and Ashgi, the
city’s god. Kesh is another, less securely located cult
Zabalam · a major sanctuary praised separately from
Umma · the goddess’s princely son and lord of
Girsu · the Lagash state’s sacred centre. Gudea’s text
names the divine sons in Ningirsu’s household. [1,7]
Civic mother, divine herald and the rulers’
protective deity in the Lagash state. [7]
Nigin · Nanshe’s Sirara sanctuary and her consort.
Another hymn gives her an unlocated sea-edge

svg.text: [1] The Temple Hymns, ETCSL 4.80.1. City-specific passages in the catalogue.
[2] ORACC, Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses; articles and scholarship
[5] Ninazu A 16–22, ETCSL 4.17.1 (Ur birth; Enegi seat).
[6] Utu B 7–12, ETCSL 4.32.2; Temple Hymns 479–493 (shrine localisation inferred).
[7] Gudea Cylinders, ETCSL 2.1.7; ETCSRI; Ragavan, CDLJ 2010:1 §3.1.1 (Lagash).
[8] ORACC RIBo / SAA royal inscriptions; Enuma Elish I 71–84; Samsu-iluna B 33–39.
[9] Nanaya for Ishbi-Erra 1–16, ETCSL 2.5.1.3; RINAP Ashurbanipal 238, obv. 4′–10′.
